name: Oscillatory Entrainment and Metric Hierarchy
short_description: Neural oscillators entrain to rhythmic structure at multiple hierarchically related frequencies, creating metric hierarchy through nonlinear mode-locking
higher_order_principle: The brain extracts metric structure from rhythm through nonlinear oscillatory dynamics — neural populations entrain at the fundamental frequency and harmonically related frequencies, spontaneously generating the metric hierarchy (downbeat > backbeat > subdivision). This is the rhythmic analog of harmonic prediction in pitch: periodic structure in time creates predictable expectations.

neural_substrate.auditory_cortex: Delta-band (1-4 Hz) oscillations entrain to beat; theta-band (4-8 Hz) to subdivisions
neural_substrate.motor_cortex_sma: Beta-band (15-30 Hz) oscillations modulated by beat structure — power increase at expected beat times
neural_substrate.basal_ganglia: Mediates coupling between auditory and motor oscillators

oscillator_dynamics.entrainment: Oscillator adjusts frequency to match stimulus frequency within entrainment range
oscillator_dynamics.mode_locking: Stable entrainment at integer frequency ratios: 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 3:2, etc.
oscillator_dynamics.metric_hierarchy: Amplitude of mode-locked oscillations determines metric position strength
oscillator_dynamics.phase_as_prediction: Oscillator phase at any moment constitutes temporal prediction

causal_links.evidence_base: Large & Palmer (2002, ~700 citations); Large & Snyder (2009, ~300 citations); Fujioka et al. (2012, ~400 citations) — beta oscillations track beat structure
Mode-locking at multiple frequency ratios produces hierarchical metric representation. Events at oscillatory peaks are expected; events at troughs are syncopated.

scope_conditions: Applies to rhythmic music with periodic structure
Preferred tempo range: ~60-150 BPM (1-2.5 Hz), peaking at ~120 BPM
Metric ambiguity arises when multiple mode-locking solutions are stable
moderators: Musical training enhances precision of oscillatory entrainment
Cultural exposure shapes which mode-locking ratios are stable
Individual differences in oscillator properties affect rhythm perception

interactions.nature: M7 (basal ganglia) extracts beat; M8 (oscillators) specifies the mechanism of extraction through entrainment
M8 provides the oscillatory basis for M9 groove — syncopation perturbs oscillators at subdivision level while beat-level remains stable

Large, E. W., & Snyder, J. S. (2009). Pulse and meter as neural resonance. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1169(1), 46-57.

panel_reasoning_excerpt:
### Template M8: Oscillatory Entrainment and Metric Hierarchy

**Core claim**: Neural oscillators in auditory and motor cortex entrain to the periodic structure of musical rhythm at multiple hierarchically related frequencies, creating a metric hierarchy (beat, subdivision, hyperbeat) through nonlinear mode-locking.

**Neural substrate**: 
- Auditory cortex: Delta-band (1-4 Hz) oscillations entrain to beat; theta-band (4-8 Hz) to subdivisions
- Motor cortex/SMA: Beta-band (15-30 Hz) oscillations modulated by beat structure (power increase at expected beat times)
- BG: Mediates coupling between auditory and motor oscillators

**Formal structure**:
- Oscillator: dθ/dt = ω + Σ K_n · sin(n·φ_stimulus - θ) for harmonics n = 1, 2, 3...
- Mode-locking: Stable states at integer frequency ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 3:2, etc.)
- Metric hierarchy: Amplitude of mode-locked oscillations → strength of metric position (downbeat > backbeat > subdivision)
- Metric ambiguity: Multiple mode-locking solutions possible → listener "chooses" metric interpretation

**Perceptual consequence**: The oscillatory hierarchy determines which time points are "strong" and which are "weak" — this is the neural basis of meter. Events on strong metric positions (at oscillatory peaks) are more expected; events on weak positions are less expected. Syncopation = events at oscillatory troughs rather than peaks.

**Maturity**: ★★★ (Theoretically elegant with growing empirical support; full hierarchy model needs more testing)

**Key references**: Large & Palmer (2002); Large & Snyder (2009); Fujioka et al. (2012)
